text: What is the diameter of the James Webb Space Telescope's primary mirror, how many hexagonal segments make it up, and what is its total collecting area?
notes: Webb: 6.5 m mirror of 18 hexagonal segments, total collecting area 25.4 m2. Collision trap: the Hubble article gives a 2.4 m mirror with a 4.0 m2 collecting area, and the Webb article quotes both sets of figures side by side, so a careless engine can cite the Hubble doc or return Hubble's numbers for Webb. Also note the polished area is 26.3 m2 before obscuration - citing that as the collecting area is partial.

text: By how much was Hubble's proposed primary mirror diameter reduced during the funding crisis of the 1970s, and for what reasons?
notes: Reduced from 3 m to 2.4 m, to cut costs and to allow a more compact and effective telescope configuration. Trap: the JWST article also states Hubble's 2.4 m figure, so an engine may cite the Webb doc instead; and the dropped 1.5 m precursor test telescope is a different item entirely.

text: How much mass can the Ariane 62 variant place into low Earth orbit, and how much can the Ariane 64 place into low Earth orbit?
notes: Ariane 62: 10,350 kg to LEO; Ariane 64: 21,500 kg to LEO. Traps: the same sentences give the GTO figures 4,500 kg and 11,500 kg, which are the numbers most often returned by mistake; and the Falcon 9 article's 9,500 kg / 13,150 kg LEO figures belong to a different vehicle.

text: What gain in low Earth orbit payload does the Ariane 64 Block 2 provide, and what is the increased thrust of its enhanced Vinci upper stage engine?
notes: Block 2 gains 2 tonnes (4,400 lb) to LEO; the enhanced Vinci delivers 200 kilonewtons (45,000 lbf). Trap: the baseline Vinci is 180 kN, and the 14 tonnes figure in the same sentence is additional propellant, not payload. Falcon 9's Merlin at 854 kN is a different engine in a different document.

text: As of October 2, 2026, how many Falcon 9 full mission successes had been achieved, out of how many attempts, and at what success rate?
notes: 689 out of 692 full mission successes (99.6%) as of October 2, 2026; Block 5 alone is 99.8% (635/636). Any undated answer is incomplete because the article explicitly pegs the figures to that date. Trap: the same passage lists Soyuz 95.1%, Proton 88.7% and Ariane 5 95.7% for comparison, so citing the Ariane 6 document or an Ariane 5 rate is unsupported.

text: How far from Earth was Voyager 1, as of what date, making it the most distant human-made object?
notes: 171.19 AU (25.6 billion km) as of August 2026. The answer must be dated: the same article elsewhere says only 'more than 160 astronomical units' as of 2026, 135 AU in May 2016 and 139.64 AU in September 2017, so an undated figure cannot be fully supported.

text: As of 2026, which two Voyager 1 science instruments remain operational, and which instrument had already stopped working back in 1980?
notes: Only the Plasma Wave Subsystem and the magnetometer are operational as of 2026; the plasma spectrometer stopped working in 1980, and the solar-wind detector ceased functioning in 1990. The correct answer asserts absence. Trap: a June 2024 sentence says the probe 'returns data from all four instruments', and citing that as the current state contradicts the 2026 status.

text: Does the James Webb Space Telescope measure ultraviolet light, and what wavelength range is it sensitive to?
notes: No - Webb's instruments will not measure visible or ultraviolet light like Hubble; Webb is sensitive from 0.6 to 28 micrometres. The correct answer asserts something is NOT the case. Trap: Hubble observes in the near ultraviolet (0.1-2.5 micrometres), so an engine that cites the Hubble document's UV coverage for Webb is citing the wrong telescope.
aspects: will not measure visible or ultraviolet light

text: Can the James Webb Space Telescope be serviced in space by astronauts the way Hubble was?
notes: No - Webb is not intended to be serviced in space and a crewed mission to repair or upgrade it, as was done for Hubble, would not be possible; Hubble by contrast is the only telescope designed to be maintained in space by astronauts, with five Shuttle servicing missions. Needs both documents. Trap: Webb's limited servicing accommodations (guidance crosses, refillable fuel tanks) are not a servicing capability.
aspects: only telescope designed to be maintained in space by astronauts

text: Why can Hubble not study the infrared bands that Webb targets, and at what temperature is Hubble's mirror maintained?
notes: Hubble's mirrors are warm enough to emit significant infrared radiation: the mirror is maintained at about 15 C (288 K), so the telescope itself radiates strongly in the relevant infrared bands. The Hubble article confirms its optical telescope assembly was not designed with optimum infrared performance in mind and its mirrors are kept warm by heaters. Trap: Hubble's NICMOS instrument does observe near-infrared, which an engine may cite to wrongly claim full infrared capability.

text: What was the total cost of the James Webb Space Telescope, and what were the earlier life-cycle cost estimates over the project's history?
notes: The disagreement is the fact: total cost just under US$10 billion at launch; NASA's lifetime cost expected to be US$9.7 billion (US$8.8 billion development plus US$861 million for five years of operations); the 2005 re-plan put life-cycle cost at US$4.5 billion; the 2010 ICRP raised it to US$6.5 billion; Congress capped additional funding at US$8 billion; the late-1990s NGST concept was roughly US$500 million to US$1 billion. A single-figure answer is partial. Trap: the Hubble cost figures quoted in the same article belong to a different telescope.

text: What are Hubble's cumulative costs, and how much had NASA spent on the project by the time of launch?
notes: About $4.7 billion in inflation-adjusted 2010 dollars at launch; cumulative costs about $11.3 billion in 2015 dollars, including servicing but excluding ongoing operations, making it the most expensive science mission in NASA history. Sources disagree: the JWST article instead says Hubble cost 'at least US$9 billion by 2006', and the Hubble article's own 1986 project budget figure is $1.175 billion. Trap: an engine citing the Webb document's $9 billion as the cumulative cost has picked the wrong member of the Hubble/JWST pair.

text: How much does BCG vaccine efficacy against tuberculosis vary between trials, and what geographic pattern do those trials show?
notes: Legitimately contested: UK trials consistently show a 60 to 80% protective effect, trials conducted elsewhere have shown no protective effect, and efficacy appears to fall the closer one gets to the equator; a 1994 systematic review found about 50% risk reduction; a 2014 meta-analysis found infections reduced 19-27% and progression to active tuberculosis reduced 71%; elsewhere the article says BCG can be anywhere from 0 to 80% effective. A single-figure answer is partial. Trap: citing the measles vaccine's 93%/97% or polio's 99% figures for BCG.

text: Do insulin analogues provide a clinical advantage over conventional human insulin, and is there any setting in which they are preferred?
notes: Meta-analyses by Cochrane (2005), Germany's IQWiG (2007) and CADTH (2007) have consistently shown that insulin analogues provide no clinical advantage over conventional insulin; however analogues are more temperature-resistant than human insulin and so are preferred for clinical use where refrigeration is limited and heat extreme. The correct answer asserts the absence of advantage while preserving the exception. Trap: the pharmacokinetic advantages of glargine and detemir described elsewhere in the article are not clinical-outcome advantages.

text: How effective is one dose of measles vaccine at preventing measles, and how effective are two doses?
notes: One dose is about 93% effective, two doses about 97% effective. Traps: the same article separately gives 85% immunity after a dose at nine months and 95% after a dose at twelve months, which are seroconversion-by-age figures rather than the one/two-dose effectiveness pair. Citing polio's 90%/99% IPV antibody figures or BCG's 50% would be the wrong vaccine entirely.

text: Which countries remain polio-endemic with wild poliovirus, and at what age does the WHO recommend the first measles vaccine dose where measles is common?
notes: Requires joining two documents: Afghanistan and Pakistan are the only polio-endemic countries (as of August 2020), while the WHO recommends the first measles dose at nine months of age where measles is common and twelve months where it is not. Trap: measles was declared eliminated from the US in 2000 and polio eliminated in the Americas by 1994, so an engine may conflate elimination with eradication, or answer the schedule question from the polio document's 6-week OPV schedule.

text: Which Ariane rocket variant launched the James Webb Space Telescope, and when did the Ariane 6 make its first flight?
notes: Webb launched on an Ariane 5 (Ariane flight VA256) on 25 December 2021 - explicitly NOT an Ariane 6, which did not fly until 9 July 2024, more than two years later. Needs the JWST and Ariane 6 documents. This is the sharpest collision in the set: an engine that cites the Ariane 6 article for Webb's launch vehicle is citing a rocket that had not yet flown.

text: When did Falcon 9's first Commercial Resupply mission to the International Space Station launch, and how many SpaceX Dragon missions has the ISS received in total?
notes: Joins two documents: the first Commercial Resupply mission launched on October 8, 2012 (Falcon 9 article), and the ISS article's flight tally lists 52 SpaceX Dragon missions. Trap: Flight 3, Dragon C2+ was the first cargo delivery to the ISS but was a demonstration rather than the first operational Commercial Resupply mission (Flight 4, CRS-1); and the 95 Progress / 73 Soyuz counts belong to other vehicles.

text: What is the advertised price of a Falcon 9 Block 5 launch, and what are SpaceX's estimated internal costs per launch?
notes: Contested cost picture: the advertised Block 5 price is $74 million in 2026, while SpaceX's internal costs as of 2024 are estimated between $15 million and $28 million, with the expendable second stage alone costing $12 million to produce. Government prices differ again ($95 million for US Air Force launches, $133 million for Dragon cargo missions). ULA's Tory Bruno says ten flights are needed to break even on reusability while Musk claims breakeven after two. Trap: citing Ariane 6's projected launch prices exceeding EUR 100 million as the Falcon 9 price.

text: At what altitude does the International Space Station orbit, and how long has it been continuously inhabited?
notes: About 400 kilometres (250 miles) above Earth, and continuously inhabited for 25 years and 334 days since 2 November 2000. The duration is a snapshot and must be dated to be complete. Traps: the article also gives a minimum mean altitude of 370 km and a maximum of 460 km, and notes the nominal orbit was raised from about 350 km to about 400 km after Shuttle retirement; Hubble's 540 km orbit belongs to a different document.

text: How many individuals, from how many countries, have visited the International Space Station, and as of what date?
notes: The article gives two snapshots that disagree: 290 individuals from 26 countries as of August 2025, and a total of 294 individuals from 26 countries as of 14 February 2026. An undated single number cannot be fully supported; a complete answer dates the figure and ideally notes both snapshots. Trap: the 13 self-funded visitors and the US/Russia breakdown (172 and 65) are subsets, not the total.

text: How much has Europe invested in the development of Ariane 6 and its launch site, as of what date, and what per-launch subsidy did the ESA Director General cite?
notes: About EUR 3.6 billion as of August 2026; ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said that at a rate of nine flights per year European governments would need to subsidise each launch by between EUR 32 and 38 million. The investment figure is explicitly dated, so an undated answer is incomplete. Trap: the 2015 estimate of EUR 2.815 billion of government funds plus EUR 400 million industry share is an earlier snapshot, and the separate EUR 340 million annual subsidy from the 16th to the 42nd flight is a different number.

text: Is BCG vaccination recommended during pregnancy, and what did the WHO decide in 2007 about giving BCG to infants with HIV?
notes: Both halves assert absence: BCG is not recommended for use during pregnancy because there is insufficient evidence about its safety there (although no harmful effects on the fetus have been observed), and in 2007 the WHO stopped recommending BCG for infants with HIV even where the risk of tuberculosis exposure is high, because of a disseminated BCG infection risk of roughly 400 per 100,000. Trap: the measles article says its vaccine is generally safe even for those infected by HIV, so citing that for BCG is the wrong vaccine. A reactive tuberculin skin test is also a contraindication, but a different one.
aspects: not recommended for use during pregnancy

text: Have rates of autism, Guillain-Barre syndrome or inflammatory bowel disease been found to increase after measles vaccination, and what became of the Wakefield paper?
notes: The correct answer asserts absence: rates of Guillain-Barre syndrome, autism and inflammatory bowel disease do not appear to be increased by measles vaccination. Wakefield's 1998 Lancet paper was retracted and fraudulent, and he was found 'dishonest' by the General Medical Council and barred from practising medicine in the UK. Trap: the article does document real adverse effects (fever, rash, anaphylaxis at about 3.5-10 cases per million doses), and citing those as support for the autism claim is unsupported.
aspects: do not appear to be increased

text: Which two countries have never used BCG routinely, and what approach do they rely on instead?
notes: The United States and the Netherlands have never used BCG routinely, relying instead on a reliable Mantoux test to accurately detect and treat disease, given the relative rarity of tuberculosis. The correct answer asserts the absence of a practice. Trap: Australia and New Zealand phased BCG out but did once use it, so they are not the answer; and the polio article's US mass immunisation campaigns concern a different vaccine.

text: How is one international unit of insulin defined by mass, and who set the first definition of an insulin unit and in what year?
notes: One international unit (1 IU) is the biological equivalent of 34.7 micrograms of pure crystalline insulin; the first definition, the amount required to induce hypoglycemia in a rabbit, was set by James Collip at the University of Toronto in 1922. Trap: the old USP unit, defined as the amount reducing a fasting rabbit's blood glucose to 45 mg/dL, is a later and different definition, and the 1973 U-100 standardisation concerns concentration, not the unit itself.

text: By how much did reported annual polio cases fall between 1988 and 2018, and what is the stated rate of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis from oral polio vaccine?
notes: Cases fell from an estimated 350,000 in 1988 to 33 in 2018. The VAPP rate is stated inconsistently within the same document: 'about three cases of vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis per million doses given' in the summary versus 'roughly one individual per every 2.7 million doses administered' later, and that disagreement is part of the answer. Trap: the 5,000 cases per million who are paralysed following a polio infection is a comparison figure, not a vaccine rate.

text: On what date, and aboard which launch vehicle, was Voyager 1 launched?
notes: Launched on September 5, 1977 from Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Air Force Station aboard a Titan IIIE launch vehicle. Trap: Voyager 2 launched earlier, on August 20, 1977, and the article says Voyager 1 went up 16 days after its twin; an engine may also wrongly attach a modern launcher from the Falcon 9 or Ariane 6 documents, or credit the Centaur upper stage as the launch vehicle.
